newsitem.title: USA: Deaf mutes to stay in U.S. during probe.
newsitem.headline: Deaf mutes to stay in U.S. during probe.

text.p: Dozens of deaf-mute Mexicans believed to have been forced to live in poverty and sell trinkets in New York City will be allowed to remain in the United States while authorities investigate, officials said on Thursday.

In what officials described as a model example of cooperation between federal and city authorities, 58 indentured labourers will continue to receive services such as medical treatment, legal aid and sign language interpreters.
The group has been living in a motel in the city borough of Queens since Saturday, when their plight was discovered.

"The Mexican nationals now in our custody are all potential material witnesses in our criminal investigation," Doris Meissner, the U.S. Immigration and Naturalisation Service commissioner, told reporters at City Hall in a conference call from Washington.

Officials rescued the deaf-mute workers from two cramped city apartments over the weekend. The workers said they were smuggeled from Mexico over the California border and transported to Los Angeles and New York.

Seven people have been arrested, including four members of one family. They are charged with conspiracy to transport and conceal illegal aliens. Authorities are still seeking the alleged ringleader, identified as Reinaldo Paoletti.
Meissner said the INS was establishing "an anti-exploitation task force" to examine leads and reports nationwide of other abuses, including coercion or extortion from immigrants.
"It is too early to determine what may come of these reports, but the INS will not tolerate the type of inhumane treatment that this case has shown," she said.
The New York ring was exposed after two deaf mutes walked into a local police station and used written notes and hand gestures to explain their situation.
Authorities believe the ringleaders recruited their victims from homes and schools for the deaf and mute in Mexico, promising them a better life in the United States.
The victims said they were forced to work seven days a week peddling trinkets on streets and subways and forced to sleep on the floor.
Some said they were physically abused if they did not make enough money selling the one-dollar keychains, baseballs, pens and toys.
Ambassador Jorge Pinto of the Mexican Consulate told reporters that Mexican and U.S. officials were working to reunite some of the people with their families.

"They want to cooperate with the investigation," Pinto said. "We have to explore what kind of bondage, what kind of psychological links these people have with them that stopped them from denouncing these crimes before."

Mexican officials have promised the victims full consular protection and legal advice. Once their status is clarified, Mexico said if they were repatriated it would help them reach their place of origin or another of their choosing.
It also promised to help them make contact with families or friends in Mexico.
Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo has vowed to punish the perpetrators of what he called such "atrocities."
